# Claims, classified

*Generated by `python eval/build_docs.py` from `eval/templates/claims.md` and `eval/results/headline.json`; every number below comes from a recorded run. `tests/test_claims.py` fails if this file is stale or if the README quotes a number that is not in the results.*

Four classes, used for every claim made about this project in the README, the documentation, the portfolio page and any launch material. A claim belongs to exactly one class:

* **VERIFIED**: a fact about the code, the tests or the recorded files that anyone can re-check from this repository without trusting a simulation (a test passes, two programs agree, a latency was measured on one machine, a defect was fixed and has a regression test).
* **SIMULATED**: a *measured* result whose meaning depends on a scripted attacker, an oracle human or a synthetic world. The measurement is real; what it says about anything outside the simulation is limited. This includes the real-model run: the model is real, the world, the planted injections and the approving humans are not.
* **LIMITATION**: a known gap, stated on purpose.
* **NOT EVALUATED**: not run. No result is claimed.

**Words this project does not use** unless evidence beyond this repository supports them: *secure*, *safe*, *robust*, *solved*, *production-ready*, *enterprise-grade*, *protects against prompt injection*. What it claims is narrower: *in this synthetic world, against these recorded attacks and these oracle humans, at this measured cost, this is what each control stopped and this is what got through*. It also does not claim to be a formal information-flow-control system (see L8).

## Simulated

Every result below was measured, and every one of them depends on what is simulated (see the note after the table).

| ID | Claim | Evidence | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | **Without a gateway, the scripted attacker reached its goal in {{scripted.cells.A0/none.attacks_reached_goal}} of {{scripted.cells.A0/none.attacks}} held-out attacks.** | `eval/results/test-scripted/` | The workload is built to exercise the vulnerability; the attacker never adapts. |
| S2 | **With Weir's defaults and a careful (oracle) human, {{scripted.cells.A3/strict.attacks_reached_goal}} of {{scripted.cells.A3/strict.attacks}} attacks reached their goal**, all of them the answer channel after a legitimate secret read ({{scripted.f4_secret_first.A3/strict.0}} of {{scripted.f4_secret_first.A3/strict.1}} such runs). The project's own "5% or less" target was **missed**. | same | Scripted attacker; oracle human; synthetic world; held-out *instances*, not held-out attack classes. |
| S3 | **With an oracle human who approves everything, {{scripted.cells.A3/careless.attacks_reached_goal}} of {{scripted.cells.A3/careless.attacks}} attacks got through under Weir's defaults; with the session rules set to deny, {{scripted.cells.A3d/careless.attacks_reached_goal}} of {{scripted.cells.A3d/careless.attacks}}; with static approval gates, {{scripted.cells.A1/careless.attacks_reached_goal}} of {{scripted.cells.A1/careless.attacks}}.** | same | The humans are deterministic oracles; no person was asked. |
| S4 | The cost to legitimate work: {{scripted.cells.A3/strict.benign_tasks_needing_approval}} of {{scripted.cells.A3/strict.benign}} designed benign tasks needed at least one approval under the defaults, against {{scripted.cells.A1/strict.benign_tasks_needing_approval}} of {{scripted.cells.A1/strict.benign}} under static gates; with the session rules set to deny, {{scripted.cells.A3d/strict.benign_tasks_needing_approval}} tasks needed one and {{scripted.cells.A3d/strict.benign_completed}} of {{scripted.cells.A3d/strict.benign}} completed. | same | Counts of designed tasks, not a usability study. |
| S5 | A tool whose definition changes after review is withheld and denied ({{scripted.rug_pull.A3.0}} of {{scripted.rug_pull.A3.1}} attacks succeed; {{scripted.rug_pull.A0.0}} of {{scripted.rug_pull.A0.1}} without a gateway). | same | Detects *changes*; a description that was malicious when reviewed is not detected. |
| S6 | **The plain session rule "no secret read after untrusted content" (`R-UNTRUSTED-READ`) was the first rule to stop the attack in {{pct:scripted.first_stop.counts.R-UNTRUSTED-READ\|scripted.first_stop.n}} of runs (A3, careful human); the destination rule (`R-DEST-UNTRUSTED`) in {{pct:scripted.first_stop.counts.R-DEST-UNTRUSTED\|scripted.first_stop.n}}, the content tracker (`R-FLOW-CONF`) in {{pct:scripted.first_stop.counts.R-FLOW-CONF\|scripted.first_stop.n}}, `R-TRIFECTA` in {{pct:scripted.first_stop.counts.R-TRIFECTA\|scripted.first_stop.n}}; in {{pct:scripted.first_stop.counts.none\|scripted.first_stop.n}} nothing was stopped (the answer channel).** | same; `docs/evaluation.md` section 3 | "First to stop" favours the rule that fires earlier in the attack (the read precedes the send). Left standing instead, with a careful human: value tier alone {{pct:scripted.cells.A2/strict.attacks_reached_goal\|scripted.cells.A2/strict.attacks}}, session tier alone {{pct:scripted.cells.A3s/strict.attacks_reached_goal\|scripted.cells.A3s/strict.attacks}}, both {{pct:scripted.cells.A3/strict.attacks_reached_goal\|scripted.cells.A3/strict.attacks}}. With an approve-everything human the session tier alone stops nothing ({{pct:scripted.cells.A3s/careless.attacks_reached_goal\|scripted.cells.A3s/careless.attacks}} left) because it asks rather than denies. |
| S7 | The content tracker alone (A2, human approves everything) let the e-mail exfiltration through in 0 of {{scripted.f1_variants.value.A2/careless.1}} runs when the value was sent verbatim, in base64, in hex or to a look-alike domain, and in {{scripted.f1_variants.rot13.A2/careless.0}} of {{scripted.f1_variants.rot13.A2/careless.1}} when it was rot13-encoded, {{scripted.f1_variants.rev.A2/careless.0}} of {{scripted.f1_variants.rev.A2/careless.1}} reversed and {{scripted.f1_variants.chunk5.A2/careless.0}} of {{scripted.f1_variants.chunk5.A2/careless.1}} sent in 5-character pieces. | `docs/evaluation.md` section 3 | Per-variant counts of a generated workload; the same attacks were all held by the session rules with a careful human. |
| S8 | **With a real small model (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507) in the loop, the attacker reached its goal in {{realmodel.cells.A0/none.attacks_reached_goal}} of {{realmodel.cells.A0/none.attacks}} unprotected runs; with Weir's defaults and a careful (oracle) human, {{realmodel.cells.A3/strict.attacks_reached_goal}} of {{realmodel.cells.A3/strict.attacks}} (all of them the answer channel).** | `eval/results/test-realmodel/` | One model, one pass per cell, greedy decoding, one machine, synthetic world, planted injections, oracle humans; says nothing about other models. The scenarios ask for the secret verbatim, so the static gates, the value tier and the defaults are indistinguishable in this run (`docs/evaluation.md` section 4). The same model completes only {{realmodel.cells.A0/none.benign_completed}} of {{realmodel.cells.A0/none.benign}} benign tasks with no gateway at all. |
| S9 | Twelve attacks written after the held-out results, with knowledge of Weir's rules, on fresh seeds (AD1 to AD12): several get through (see L2, L3). | `docs/red-team.md`; `eval/results/adaptive/` | Five runs per cell; written by the system's author; not held out. |

**What is simulated.** The attacker follows every injection and persists after a block; it does not adapt to what the gateway says (except in S9). The "careful human" and the "human who approves everything" are deterministic oracles; no person was asked. The world is invented: mailbox, files, web pages and notes; the secrets are random strings generated per scenario; addresses use reserved example domains. In S8 the model is real but the injections are planted by the scenario generator and the humans are still oracles.

## Limitations

| ID | Statement |
|---|---|
| L1 | **The answer channel is out of reach.** A model that was legitimately given a secret and then reads an injection can repeat it in its reply; Weir never sees the reply. It reached its goal in 100% of its runs under every arm. |
| L2 | **The value tier is a heuristic.** `rot13`, reversal, spelled-out digits, look-alike letters, pieces shorter than the match length, fingerprints and wrapped encodings pass it (measured in `docs/evaluation.md` and AD2 to AD12 in `docs/red-team.md`). |
| L3 | **Data in a target argument is not scanned** (AD4, AD5); **state changes that never name their target are not flagged** (AD9, AD10); **the approval screen cannot tell the user's e-mail from the attacker's** (AD11). Found after the freeze and documented, not fixed. |
| L4 | **The session tier costs usability** and a wrong label, a missing content declaration or an undeclared egress tool in the policy is a bypass. |
| L5 | One small model, one machine; synthetic data; toy tools; English only; one AI-assisted author for the system, the scenarios, the oracles and the red-team; no independent review; never deployed; no users. |
| L6 | Tools over stdio only. No resources, prompts, sampling, HTTP transports or authentication. |
| L7 | The idea is established (the lethal trifecta, Meta's Rule of Two, CaMeL, FIDES, vendor MCP gateways, small open-source projects). Nothing here claims novelty or superiority; none of them was run for comparison. |
| L8 | **Not a formal information-flow-control system.** Labels are coarse, declared by an operator and only as good as the declaration; the content tracker is a heuristic; there is no non-interference guarantee and no proof. "Information-flow" describes the design vocabulary, not a verified property. |
| L9 | **Held-out means held-out instances.** New seeds from the same generator after a freeze, not new attack classes. |

## Not evaluated

| ID | Not run |
|---|---|
| N1 | Any hosted or frontier model. |
| N2 | Any commercial MCP host (the official SDK client and one third-party server were used). |
| N3 | Any real person approving anything; approval fatigue. |
| N4 | Real data, real accounts, real enterprise integrations, OAuth or SSO. |
| N5 | Throughput, concurrency at scale, long-running soak behaviour, memory use over days. |
| N6 | Multi-tenant operation, authentication, rate limiting. |
| N7 | An independent code review or penetration test. |
| N8 | A head-to-head comparison with CaMeL, FIDES or any other gateway. |
